questions.q: What does Row-Level Security (RLS) restrict, and how does that differ from Dynamic Data Masking?
options: RLS restricts which rows a query is allowed to see or affect, based on a predicate; DDM instead changes how a column's value is displayed without hiding entire rows
RLS and DDM restrict exactly the same thing — column display
RLS restricts which columns exist in a table's schema
RLS only applies to backup files, never to live queries
questions.explain: Two users with identical table-level SELECT permission can get entirely different row sets under RLS — that's the axis it operates on.

questions.q: What are the two objects that together implement Row-Level Security on a table?
options: A predicate function (an inline table-valued function) and a security policy that binds it to the table as FILTER and/or BLOCK
A firewall rule and a Virtual Network rule
A Column Master Key and a Column Encryption Key
A masking function and an UNMASK grant
questions.explain: CREATE FUNCTION defines the predicate logic; CREATE SECURITY POLICY binds it to a specific table.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between a FILTER predicate and a BLOCK predicate?
options: A FILTER predicate silently narrows what SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE return with no error; a BLOCK predicate actively rejects a write operation that would violate the rule, throwing an error
They are functionally identical, just named differently
A FILTER predicate only applies to INSERT statements
A BLOCK predicate silently hides rows, while FILTER throws errors
questions.explain: BLOCK is what stops a sales rep from inserting a row claiming a SalesRepID that isn't their own — FILTER alone wouldn't necessarily catch that on INSERT.

questions.q: Why might a report unexpectedly returning fewer rows than expected be CORRECT behavior rather than a bug?
options: Because a Row-Level Security FILTER predicate may be silently narrowing the result set for that user's session, which looks identical to a data or join problem unless you know the policy exists
Because SQL Server always caps SELECT * results at 1,000 rows by default
Because Dynamic Data Masking always removes rows entirely instead of masking values
Because Always Encrypted blocks any query returning more than one encrypted column
questions.explain: RLS is transparent to the application — no error, no indication anything was filtered — which is exactly why documenting policies matters.

questions.q: Does Row-Level Security require any changes to the querying application's code?
options: No — the application still runs an ordinary SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE, and the security policy transparently narrows what's returned or allowed
Yes — every query must be rewritten to include an explicit WHERE clause matching the predicate
Yes — RLS only works with stored procedures, never ad-hoc queries
RLS requires the application to authenticate using Always Encrypted-aware drivers
questions.explain: This transparency is exactly like TDE and DDM — powerful because one policy protects every application uniformly, risky if the policy's existence is forgotten.
